_comment_title: Where this show parts company with the packs cut to the same design.
Hall of Femme sets its captions in Telegraf - a 200-weight hairline
for the block, the 800 for a picked word - on a hot pink card. This
one sets them in Forma DJR Display Extra Bold, with ITC American
Typewriter Bold for a picked word, on a deep blue one, and it is the
only pack under this heading whose card has square corners.
The two faces are the decision the rest of the pack follows from, and
the pairing is a kind no sibling has: every one of them picks a word
out with another cut of the SAME family - a weight, or a slant. This
one changes family outright, from a display grotesque to a slab
serif.
It is not a free choice, and the constraint is worth stating because
it is what a reader will otherwise try to relax. A highlight here has
only three languages available - colour, weight, or face. Colour is
spent: `colors` below hands both colours to the user, and `text`
reaches the highlight along with the block, so a highlight that
recoloured would be recoloured out from under itself. Weight is spent
too, and that is the part that is new: the block is already an Extra
Bold, so there is no heavier cut of it to reach for. Hall of Femme
could go 200 to 800 precisely because it started at the bottom of its
family; a pack that starts at the top has to change something else.
What is left is the face, and a slab serif against a display
grotesque is the loudest version of that there is. It changes the
shape of every letter rather than its weight, so a picked word reads
as a different KIND of statement - stamped, typed, on the record -
which is the register a show about charges and verdicts wants. It is
the technique laugh-society-2 uses under the Binge heading, where a
picked line in an upright face reads as somebody else speaking,
applied to a word instead of a line.
It costs what a second face always costs, and the cost is documented
rather than absorbed: everything about a picked word is measured in
its OWN face (`styleFor` in js/text.js), both faces are loaded and
verified before the channel is drawn with, and a missing one is named
in the fontguard banner by itself. See the `highlight.face` section of
content/README.md.
The card is kept, as it is on every pack under this heading, and here
it is not doing the job it does on Hall of Femme. There the card and
the hairline are one decision: a 200-weight face over an unknown
photograph disappears, and the card is what makes that weight a choice
instead of a risk. An Extra Bold display face needs no such rescuing.
The card stays because it is the form this design IS, a statement laid
on the picture rather than words burned into it, and because the six
colours below are the show's look and there is nowhere else to put
them.

_comment_color: The channel's own answer, and therefore what every frame is set
in until somebody presses a swatch: a frame stores no colour of
its own until it is given one, and this is what it falls back to
(see state.textColorFor). It is one of the six in `colors` below,
so the white swatch is the one that shows as chosen on an
untouched frame - the swatch is found by matching this value
rather than by being listed first.
White letters on the deep blue card is the pairing this show opens
on: the blue is the brand, so it is the CARD - the shape that is a
fifth of the frame and reads before anything on it - and the type
is what has to stay legible against it.
White rather than black, which is where this pack parts company
with the siblings that open dark on a bright card. #021A91 is not
a bright card. It is a very dark blue, nearer to black than any of
the other five colours here, so black on it is barely a contrast
at all - it is the one pairing in this palette that fails outright
rather than merely reading quietly. Of what is left, white is the
loudest and the most neutral; #FFD400 on the same card is the
louder-still alternative and is one swatch away, along with the
other thirty-four.
_comment_colors: The six colours this show is set in, offered for the letters and
for the card behind them - six buttons each in the title panel
(see editor.renderColorButtons). Nothing counts the lists and the
row wraps, so a palette is as long as a pack wants it; four is
what the first packs under this heading happened to want, not a
number the feature has.
The same six in both lists, deliberately, and for the reason Hall
of Femme states: the point is the PAIRING. Thirty-six combinations
of a black, a white, a pale grey, a deep blue, a red and a yellow
- and unlike a palette of four, this one is not an argument that
every pairing is worth having. It is an argument that which ones
are worth having is not knowable in advance, because it depends on
the photograph the card is lying on.
The six are three pairs rather than six colours. Absolute black
and absolute white are the ends, and the exact values matter for
the reason every pack under this heading gives: a near-black that
reads as black on a monitor becomes a grey slab beside a genuinely
black picture on a phone, and an off-white card is a dirty one
against a blown highlight. The card is a flat shape, not a
photograph seen through it, so there is nothing for either extreme
to be too harsh against.
#DBDBE6 is the quiet one - a pale grey with just enough blue in it
to belong to #021A91 rather than to sit beside it - and it is here
so the show has a card that is not shouting, which is what a long
caption over a busy still wants.
#021A91, #DB051F and #FFD400 are the loud three, and they are
spaced across the wheel rather than around one hue, which is what
makes each of them work in both roles: a blue dark enough to be a
ground for the other two, a red at full saturation and middling
brightness which is the one colour here that works better as ink
than as a card, and a yellow bright enough both to be ink on the
blue and to be a card the black sits on. Three colours of similar
brightness would have given a great many pairings that are all the
same pairing.
Nothing stops the user setting white on white, or blue on blue.
That is not an oversight: the two lists are independent because
the pairing is the feature, and a rule barring the six matching
combinations - or the several more that are near enough to
matching to be unreadable - would cost the panel more explaining
than an invisible caption costs the user, who can see it is
invisible and presses another swatch.
`text` reaches the highlight as well as the block - see the note
on `colors` in js/channels.js. This channel's highlight is a
different FACE and not a different colour, so what colour the type
is has one answer and not two.
_comment_highlight: A picked word is set in ITC American Typewriter Bold, in the same
colour as the rest of the block. Why the face and not the weight
is argued in `_comment_title` above: the block is already an Extra
Bold, so there is nothing heavier to reach for, and the slab serif
changes the shape of the letters instead.
The colour it names is the block's, so the recolour draws exactly
what its neighbours are drawn in and the face is the whole of the
difference. Stated all the same, for the fallback reason `color`
above is stated - a highlight that changed colour as well as face
would be two highlights.
The mode and the scope come from the preset, which is where the
argument for picking out words rather than lines lives.
One consequence is this pack's own, and it is why the preset's
stated `fontSize` matters more here than on a single-family pack.
The Typewriter is the wider of the two faces at the same size, so
a picked word makes its line longer. At a stated size that is all
it does - the line breaks one word earlier and nothing is resized.
Under a size fit it would have retyped the block around the word
being emphasised, and worse than on a sibling: a block takes one
size, from whichever line needs the smallest one, so a picked word
in the wider face could have set the size for every line including
the ones it is not on (see content/README.md). Stating the size is
what makes two families on one block safe, as well as what makes
forty stills one set.
_comment_panel: Deep blue, and square. The fill is what every pack under this
heading states for itself - it is the one thing about the card
that IS the brand - and the radius is this pack's exception, which
the preset asks to be explained where it is taken.
The blue is the card and not the letters because it is the brand
and the card is the bigger surface: a fifth of the frame, read
before anything set on it. This and `color` above are also the
only place the opening look is stated, since the two lists in
`colors` are written in one order so the two rows of buttons read
as the same palette twice - which means neither of them can decide
what an untouched frame wears.
The radius is 0 against the preset's 13, and it contradicts a
sentence written for every other channel here: that a
square-cornered slab reads as a crop or a letterbox, something the
player did, while a rounded one reads as a graphic somebody made.
That argument is right and this show takes the other side of it on
purpose. A rounded corner is a soft, conversational, social shape;
a square one is a document. This is a show about charges and
verdicts, set in a display grotesque and picked out in a typewriter
face - the whole look is paperwork read aloud, and a card with
rounded corners is the one part of it that would read as a chat
bubble.
The letterbox risk the 13 protects against is also much smaller
here than it is there, because it is a risk for a card in a
NEUTRAL colour and five of these six are not neutral. A square
block of #DB051F across the foot of a still is not something
anybody mistakes for the player. It is a real risk for the two
that are neutral, and the honest version of this note is that a
black card with square corners on a dark still can look like a
crop - which is a pairing the user chose and can leave in one
press, and a smaller cost than rounding the other four.
Nothing else about the card is stated. Its shape, its padding, its
border and its shadow are the Snapchat caption design and come
from the preset, including the border colour that is never drawn -
and which, at radius 0, has one less thing to do: it is there to
stop the outer rectangle blending into a pale rim along a ROUNDED
edge. Left in place regardless, because it is the preset's answer
and this pack has no reason of its own to hold a copy of it.

_comment_branding: No dark gradient. It exists to hold a title legible against the
photograph, and this title is not against the photograph at all - it
is on a card of its own. A scrim over every still would darken forty
pictures to solve a problem the card has already solved.
